newsitem.title: FRANCE: Ramadan killings cause despair in Algeria.
newsitem.headline: Ramadan killings cause despair in Algeria.

text.p: Haunted by killings in the Moslem month of Ramadan in which about 300 people have died, Algerians have begun to despair of an end to five years of violence.

Political analysts say the attacks, which Algiers blames on Moslem fundamentalists, changed little in the power conflict in the North African country. Neither Moslem rebels nor the security forces were any nearer to a military solution.
President Liamine Zeroual and the generals were pursuing an unchanged political strategy, said one.
"Those behind the killings have shown they are capable of a lot of things and they are getting more capable," said analyst Martin Stone, of the London-based Control Risks organisation.
"But there is no less likelihood of elections in May or June and no less likelihood of the same people winning."
Algeria has been without a parliament since January 1992 when the authorites cancelled an election in which the Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) had a commanding lead.

One regional diplomatic source said: "Our sense is that Ramadan violence has had a severe psychological impact on the government's sense of confidence, particularly after its statement that 'terrorism is residual'."
Foreign governments have expressed alarm at the bombs and massacres, but they have kept out of the conflict.
The United States, urged to help by Algerian war veteran Hocine Ait Ahmed, leader of the Socialist Forces Front (FFS), said this would need an invitation from Algiers.
Algeria's leaders always rejects foreign "interference".
France, a powerful financial supporter of Algeria, ignored French opposition calls for mediation in the conflict.
"Algeria's fate is not decided in Paris," French Prime Minister Alain Juppe said last Thursday, despite "feeling of horror in the face of so much barbarity".
The spate of Ramadan bombs and the killing of trade union boss Abdelhak Benhamouda followed a speech by Zeroual in which he vowed that "terrorism" would be finally eradicated.
But he gave no strategy for this or a date for a promised general election which the authorities see as a way to end the crisis.
"Never have we spent such a terrible Ramadan, a month that is supposed to be one of joy," a middle-aged woman said as the period drew to an end. "...it has become a calvary."

Algeria has experienced other Ramadans where bloodshed brought despair. But Ramadan this year, with at least eight bombs in the capital and 17 defused, and a series of massacres with up to 38 people being slaughtered in a single night of terror, has been marked by its sheer intensity.
Despite the bloodshed and terror, Ramadan saw no decrease in foreign business confidence in the country as far as oil and gas companies were concerned, Stone of Control Risks said.
OPEC-member Algeria relies for around 95 percent of its foreign income on oil and gas sales abroad.
"Business has looked on (the violence) indifferently. As long as it's not happening in the Sahara (desert)," he said, referring to the nation's main oil and gas producing regions.
The complexes are well guarded, with no-go zones limiting access, and a new airfield enabling foreign and other workers to avoid the dangerous drive south.
But for Algerian residents in the north, from cities to hamlets, Ramadan remains a nightmare hanging over the future.
"When we say it has been bad, we mean on every level," commented one, saying that even the special cakes for the month no longer contained almonds because they were too dear.
"Before this year we used to get into debt almost with pleasure, to buy new clothes and things for the children. We did things we couldn't do the rest of the year.
"It was the sole month when women could go out alone in the evening. You saw people you didn't see the rest of the time.
"But now not only are there are no more of these pleasures, there is death."
